source: Cameron, Hendon et al. (2020) Systematically improving espresso: insights from mathematical modeling and experiment. Matter 2, 631-648. doi:10.1016/j.matt.2019.12.019
what: Espresso on an EK43 grinder, 6 bar water pressure, 98 N tamp. Fig. 4: shot time and extraction yield vs grind setting GS (smaller GS = finer). Fig. 2B: volume particle size distributions at GS 2.5, 2.0, 1.5, 1.0.
fig4_provenance: Fig. 4 is vector. Marker centres and error-bar ends read from the PDF drawing commands; axes from the tick-mark lines. Error-bar midpoints agree with marker centres to 0.01. Overlay: cameron2020_fig4_overlay.png. Bars are +-1 standard deviation (figure legend). Two shot-time bars are hidden inside markers (sd not readable, null).
paper_finding: Homogeneous-flow model predicts EY rising monotonically as the grind gets finer; measured EY peaks at GS 1.7 and falls for finer grinds (regime 2, partially clogged / inhomogeneous flow). 9 bar clogged at fine settings, so they used 6 bar.
fig2b_provenance: Fig. 2B is vector. Each outlined curve sampled from its Bezier path; x from the log-axis tick labels (1, 10, 100, 1000 um), y from the 0-20 % labels. Curve-to-GS assignment by the paper's statement that finer grinding increases fines and reduces boulder size. Overlay: cameron2020_fig2b_overlay.png.
text_facts: Fig. 2A caption: at GS 2.5, 99 % of particles are < 100 um and account for 80 % of the surface area. Fines size stays constant as GS falls; their proportion rises.
